Empirical Research Plan  
“School Quality, School Lotteries, and Crime”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Strategy: Two–Stage Least Squares (Instrumental‐Variables).

Why IV?  
• The Charlotte-Mecklenburg choice program assigns lottery numbers randomly.  
• Some winners do not actually enroll in the assigned higher-quality school and some losers may still switch by other means ⇒ non-compliance.  
• Using “lottery offer” (intent-to-treat; ITT) as an instrument for “attendance at a higher-quality school” delivers the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) for compliers.  
• Randomization ensures instrument exogeneity; the IV framework deals with imperfect take-up.

Extensions:  
• Cohort-by-age event-study of crime trajectories (years since lottery) using the same instrument.  
• Heterogeneity by gender, race, baseline test scores.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable (second stage):  
T_i = 1 if student i actually attends a “high-quality” middle/high school in the entry year (e.g., top quartile of the district quality index or schools with value-added > median).

Instrument (first stage):  
Z_i = 1 if student i received an offer from a high-quality school in the lottery they listed as their first choice.

Control group (counterfactual):  
Students who did not receive such an offer (Z_i = 0). They are observable because they also entered the lottery.

Treatment timing / event date:  
t = fall semester following the spring lottery in grade 5 (transition to middle school) or grade 8 (transition to high school), depending on cohort. Outcome window: from assignment year up to roughly age 30 crime records.

No running variable & cutoff needed (not RDD).

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Random Assignment / Independence  
   Lottery numbers are random conditional on application choices ⇒ Z ⟂ unobservables. Highly plausible; testable via balance checks.

A2. First-Stage Relevance  
   Winning the lottery meaningfully raises attendance at a higher-quality school. Plausible; can be verified (F-stat > 10).

A3. Exclusion Restriction  
   Lottery offer affects future crime only through actual school attended, not through other channels (e.g., psychological effects of winning). Plausible given limited information content of an offer; discuss possible family relocation responses.

A4. Monotonicity (No Defiers)  
   No student is less likely to attend a good school because they win the lottery. Plausible.

A5. SUTVA / No Spillovers  
   One student’s offer does not change another’s criminal outcomes except through own treatment. Could be violated via peer spillovers; addressed by clustering and robustness (see §4).

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Differential Mobility / Attrition  
   Families who win may move districts; losers may exit public schools.  
   → Track students in statewide arrest and enrollment files; show balanced attrition rates; use Lee bounds if attrition is differential.

T2. Spillovers & General Equilibrium Effects  
   Losers may remain in lower-quality schools whose peer composition changes.  
   → Document neighborhood-school peer changes; perform “leave-one-out” analysis at the school-grade-cohort level; cluster SEs at lottery-cohort × school to allow for correlated errors.

T3. Multiple Applications / Preference Lists  
   Randomization is conditional on rank-ordered list; strategic ranking could correlate with unobservables.  
   → Include fixed effects for application cohort × first-choice school; restrict to students listing at least one high-quality option.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# PACKAGES
library(data.table)    # fast data handling
library(fixest)        # IV regressions
library(modelsummary)  # nice tables

# 5.1. DATA LOADING
dt <- fread("charlotte_lottery_1996_1999.csv")

# 5.2. VARIABLE CONSTRUCTION
# School quality index already in file: 'school_quality'
qcut <- quantile(dt$school_quality, .75, na.rm = TRUE)
dt[, high_quality := as.integer(school_quality >= qcut)]

# Instrument: offer from a high-quality school
dt[, offered_high := as.integer(lottery_offer == 1 & high_quality == 1)]

# Actual treatment: attended a high-quality school in entry grade
dt[, attend_high  := as.integer(enrolled_school_quality >= qcut)]

# Main outcome: ever arrested by age 25
dt[, arrest25 := as.integer(first_arrest_age <= 25)]

# 5.3. MAIN 2SLS SPECIFICATION
iv_main <- feols(arrest25 ~ 1 | attend_high ~ offered_high,
                 data = dt,
                 cluster = ~lottery_cohort)

summary(iv_main)

# 5.4. BALANCE (COVARIATE) CHECK
covars <- c("male","black","hispanic","baseline_math","baseline_reading","free_lunch")
bal_formula <- reformulate("offered_high", covars)
bal_results <- lapply(covars, function(v){
   feols(as.formula(paste(v, "~ offered_high")), data = dt)
})
modelsummary(bal_results, gof_omit = "Adj|AIC|BIC",
             title = "Balance on Pre-Treatment Covariates")

# 5.5. ROBUSTNESS: AGE-YEAR EVENT STUDY
# Create years-since-lottery dummies
for(y in -1:10) dt[, paste0("year",y) := as.integer(years_since_lottery == y)]
es_formula <- reformulate(paste0("year", -1:10), "attend_high")
iv_es <- feols(arrest ~ . | attend_high ~ offered_high,
               data = dt, cluster = ~lottery_cohort)
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Economic theory (human-capital plus incapacitation/peer-environment channels) suggests a negative effect: attending a higher-quality school lowers later criminal activity. Based on prior charter/choice studies, expect a 20–30 percent reduction in probability of ever being arrested by age 25 for compliers (baseline mean ≈ 15 %). Elasticity roughly −0.2.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Strong first stage (F-stat > 10) ................. 1  
C2: Independence / Randomization of Z ................ 1  
C3: Exclusion restriction plausible .................. 0.5  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) ........................ 1  
C5: SUTVA (no spillovers) ............................ 0.5  
TOTAL (max = 5) ...................................... 4/5

────────────────────────────────────────
End of Plan
